newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Housing mkt to escape UK budget unscathed.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Housing mkt to escape UK budget unscathed.

text.p: Taxes on British property transactions are expected to be left unchanged in the budget due to be unveiled on July 2, a Reuters survey showed on Wednesday.

In the survey of 20 British economists, carried out between June 19 and 20, 11 said Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown would leave mortgage interest tax relief (MIRAS) at 15 percent on the first 30,000 sterling of a mortgage. The other nine respondents expected some kind of reduction in the relief.
Thirteen said they expected stamp duty -- a levy on property transactions -- to remain at one percent on properties worth 60,000 sterling or more. The other seven expected stamp duty to rise.

"This budget is really only a mini-budget and we expect personal taxes to be left unchanged. There is a chance tax bands may be revised at a later stage," said Edmund Nonis, economist at Nikko Europe.
Analysts also said the chancellor would need to think carefully about any proposals for generating revenue from property taxes.
Abolition of MIRAS would have a particularly detrimental effect on areas outside London, where the property market is just beginning to show signs of recovery, they said.

"Many first time buyers are already being hit by higher interest rates of which there are more to come. Stamp duty is also another major cost to account for," one contributor, who declined to be named, said.

The Bank of England's monetary policy committee raised official interest rates to 6.5 percent from 6.25 percent on June 6, leading mortgage companies to increase their home loan rates. Many analysts are expecting another 25 basis point rise in official rates at the meeting of the policy committee on July 10.

Most of those who expect the government to reduce MIRAS or increase stamp duty see it as an attempt to curb run-away consumer spending, following a spate of building society mergers and flotations which have given many British consumers an injection of cash.

"Whatever the mechanism, there is recognition the economy has to be cooled down. With increases in property taxes, people will have to think twice about moving," said Mike Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers.
"Most people believe MIRAS is going. It's only a question of timing, we think it will be phased out."
Some of those surveyed expected stamp duty to be raised, while MIRAS is left unchanged.

"MIRAS has more of an impact on home-owners at the lower end of the market. But an increase in stamp duty would sit well with the (Labour) party faithful," said Adrian Owens, economist at Julius Baer investments.
"It would penalise those with relatively expensive properties. They could differentiate further by possibly increasing stamp duty on property valued at over 100,000 sterling, for example," he said.
Britain's Labour party won an overwhelming mandate to govern on May 1, after 18 years of Conservative rule.
Another reason given by contributors for an increase in stamp duty was synchronisation with the European Union (EU). The equivalent tax in most of Europe is between six and eight percent.

The government seems to be making a move towards joining European economic and monetary union (EMU) at some stage if not on January 1, 1999, they noted. So longer term interest rates would have to fall to European levels, said Mihir Warty, economist at the Centre for Economics and Business Research.
"If British interest rates fall to European levels, this will encourage more borrowing. One way to counteract this is to increase the tax on property transfers," he said.
Just six of the 20 contributors expected insurance premium tax, currently at four percent, to be increased.
A majority of contributors, 17 out of 20 in each case, expected capital gains tax and inheritance tax to remain unchanged.
